We tackle a challenge in monitoring linguistic evolution through word embeddings, where a small change in a word's semantic meaning can significantly impact its contextual variance. To address this, we introduce the "modified scenario" of a classical semantic shift problem, where animals ranked by size need to be restructured following a domain change. We evaluate the performance of three context types (nominal, modified nominal, and full contextual information) using two popular embedding tools (Word2Vec and GloVe). Our results show that within the standard framework, a slight change in contextual variance can lead to inaccurate recommendations for reordering animals. To rectify this, we propose an innovative approach called "Domain-Aware Reordering" that seamlessly integrates a permutation algorithm with the existing framework, allowing for more precise reordering based on domain-specific characteristics. We further develop a "Within-List Adjustment" strategy to further optimize the results. Our domain-aware approach outperforms the standard framework and established methods, resulting in significant improvements in reordering animals and demonstrating its broad applicability across various embedding tools and context types. We also introduce an analytical model to illustrate how changes in contextual variance impact the stability of semantic shifts, providing valuable insights into the behavior of word embeddings in context. Our code is available on GitHub, and we hope our research paves the way for developing more effective methods to monitor linguistic evolution through word embeddings.
